HelioSupport to send Redwood 2 example request IDs from yesterday’s spike where they saw confusing errors.
Redwood to enable a draft “deny reason code” header for HelioSupport in pilot (if safe) and confirm exact strings.
Redwood to follow up on per-tenant burst reject panel visibility in the customer-facing console (ETA / interim dashboard export).

Peter Holtz - Pull traces for the 07/01 08:10-08:25 PT window and confirm whether denials were policy vs pool saturation - Due 2025-07-03
Logan Wright - Confirm which metric dimensions are safe to expose to customer (tenant+region, exclude model to avoid cardinality) - Due 2025-07-05

summary: Weekly burst beta check-in with HelioSupport. Customer reported predictable morning spikes and saw ~8–15% burst denials during a 10–20 minute window in us-east, plus confusing error behavior (mix of 503 and 429; unclear whether to retry). Redwood reviewed current guardrails (per-tenant TPS/concurrency caps, cooldown, global circuit breaker) and agreed to tighten customer-facing messaging and provide explicit deny reason codes/headers. Redwood to investigate whether denials were driven by pool saturation vs policy limits and to share updated retry guidance.
topics:
1) Observed spike pattern + burst usage windows
2) Burst admission: deny rates, cooldown behavior, saturation gates
3) Error semantics (429 vs 503) + customer retry guidance
4) Dashboards/visibility (reject reasons, pool health)
5) Shadow metering and how burst usage is attributed during pilot
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcription

Title: Burst beta pilot - weekly check-in (rejects + error messaging)
Date: 2025-07-02
Time: 09:00 AM - 09:41 AM PT
Duration: 41 minutes

Attendees
- Miguel Santos (Redwood Inference, Pilot Success)
- Peter Holtz (Redwood Inference, SRE Embed)
- Logan Wright (Redwood Inference, Telemetry)
- Sara Kim (HelioSupport, Platform Eng)
- David Chen (HelioSupport, SRE)
- Anita Rao (HelioSupport, ML Eng)

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, cool. I think we’re good. This is the weekly burst beta check-in. Sara, David, Anita — thanks for jumping on. We’ve got Peter and Logan here as well. Um, agenda wise, I wanted to cover what you saw in the last week, especially the morning spike and the reject rates you mentioned in Slack. And then we can talk about error messages and what we’re changing.

[00:22] Sara Kim: Yep. Sounds good.

[00:24] David Chen: Yeah, thanks.

[00:26] Miguel Santos: Before we dive in, quick status from our side: we didn’t change any burst policy defaults in your tenant since last Friday. So whatever behavior you’re seeing is likely traffic shape plus pool conditions, not config drift. Peter has been watching the pool saturation board.

[00:41] Peter Holtz: Yeah. I pulled a couple graphs but I’d like request IDs from you to be sure we’re looking at the same thing.

[00:47] Miguel Santos: Great. Sara, do you want to walk through the spike pattern? Like, what’s “normal” and then what happened yesterday?

[00:55] Sara Kim: Sure. So, we have a pretty predictable weekday spike. It’s basically 7:50 to maybe 8:30 AM Pacific, it’s when our east coast customer base logs in and we run like a bunch of… I don’t know, queue drains? It’s a mix of interactive chat plus some background summarization jobs.

[01:13] Sara Kim: Baseline dedicated capacity is fine most of the day. The burst is mainly there for that 20-ish minute window. We saw, yesterday, from our side, a burst deny rate around… I’m looking at our client metrics… about 12% at peak for a few minutes. The rest of the time it was like, low single digits.

[01:32] David Chen: And it wasn’t just denies. It’s the confusion on what to do. Some requests came back as 503 and some as 429. And our retry layer treats those differently. So we ended up with some weird retry storms.

[01:45] Miguel Santos: Got it. That’s helpful. When you say deny, was it explicit “burst denied” or just any non-200?

[01:52] Sara Kim: On our side we’re counting non-200 from the Dedicated endpoint. We can split by status code. Most were 429, some 503. And a handful were like 524, but that might be Cloudflare on our side — not sure.

[02:08] Peter Holtz: Okay. That fits what we’ve been discussing internally. The 503s are likely “no capacity available” style responses. But I don’t want to guess, we need to see the deny reason codes from our logs.

[02:19] Miguel Santos: Can you share a couple request IDs after the call? Even two is enough. Ideally from that 8:10 to 8:25 PT window.

[02:27] Sara Kim: Yeah, we can do that.

[02:29] Miguel Santos: Cool. Anita, from the ML side, anything you noticed? Like quality shifts or latency changes during burst?

[02:36] Anita Rao: Quality is okay. We’re still pinned to the same model version. Latency is… it’s hard to say because the denies kind of dominate. For the successful ones, I think p50 was stable. p95 got a bit worse, but it’s within what we expected. Like maybe 150 to 200 milliseconds worse at the tail.

[02:55] David Chen: The bigger pain is operational. Our oncall sees a spike in errors and it’s not obvious if it’s “our dedicated is down” or “burst got denied.”

[03:05] Miguel Santos: Yeah, that’s exactly the gap we want to close before GA. Okay. Peter, can you explain briefly how denial happens today in the pilot? Just so we’re aligned.

[03:14] Peter Holtz: Sure. So think of it as: request comes in, we try to serve on your baseline dedicated pool first. If baseline is saturated beyond your reserved concurrency, we attempt the burst path — but only if your tenant is eligible, the region pool has headroom, and you’re within the configured per-tenant burst caps.

[03:34] Peter Holtz: Those caps are basically two things right now: concurrency and tokens-per-second. There’s also a cooldown to avoid oscillation, which kicks in if you exceed the caps or if the pool trips the global saturation gate. When any of those are hit, the admission decision is “deny burst,” and then routing either falls back or returns an error, depending on request type and your settings.

[03:56] Sara Kim: When you say “falls back,” do you mean it can go to hosted or a different region? Because we were told it would stay in the region.

[04:05] Miguel Santos: Great question. In your pilot config, we do not route you to hosted and we don’t cross-region without explicit allow. So practically speaking: baseline then burst pool in the same region. If burst is denied, we return an error to the client. There is some nuance around which error code, and that’s part of what we’re fixing.

[04:24] David Chen: Okay. So for us there’s no “secret fallback” happening.

[04:26] Miguel Santos: Correct.

[04:28] Logan Wright: And from telemetry side, we do log whether it was baseline vs burst and why it was denied. We’re just not surfacing it cleanly to you yet.

[04:37] Sara Kim: Right. That’s what we want.

[04:40] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk numbers. Sara said 12% non-200. Peter, what did you see in Redwood dashboards for that window?

[04:48] Peter Holtz: I saw the us-east burst pool saturation gauge go up, not full red but like, trending high — around 0.85 for a few minutes. At the same time, HelioSupport’s tenant-level burst admit rate dropped. The pattern looked like a mix: some denies due to tenant TPS cap, some due to pool gate. But I need the request IDs to confirm.

[05:10] David Chen: Is that pool shared with the hosted fleet? Like are we competing with hosted users?

[05:15] Miguel Santos: The burst pool is controlled shared, but it’s isolated from core hosted commitments. The intent is: it can’t cannibalize the hosted SLOs. So we reserve headroom separately. You are competing with other burst-enabled tenants in that region, yes, but with fairness and hard caps.

[05:33] David Chen: Okay, so it’s shared with other “burst” customers but not like general public.

[05:36] Miguel Santos: Exactly.

[05:39] Sara Kim: That’s fine. We just need predictability. Like if we’re buying this add-on, we can’t have 12% denies every morning.

[05:47] Miguel Santos: Totally. Our success metric for pilot is more like “admission succeeds for the contracted burst envelope most of the time,” and when it doesn’t, we can explain it and you can tune. So the first question is: are we under-provisioned in the pool for the region, or are your caps too tight, or is your spike shape sharper than what we modeled.

[06:10] Sara Kim: Our spike is sharp, yeah. It’s a bunch of concurrent requests that come in within like 60 seconds.

[06:16] Peter Holtz: That can trip cooldown if it looks like a thundering herd.

[06:19] David Chen: Can you explain cooldown? Because I saw a pattern where we get a deny, then for like a minute we keep getting denied even though our load goes down.

[06:27] Peter Holtz: Yeah. That’s basically intentional. If we see you exceed burst caps, we back off admission for a short period. It’s like a circuit breaker but tenant-scoped. It prevents rapid admit/deny oscillation which is bad for the pool and for latency.

[06:44] David Chen: Okay, but it means we need to make our retry logic smarter. Right now we just retry on 503 immediately and on 429 we do like, 250 milliseconds backoff. If it’s a one-minute cooldown, that’s pointless.

[06:58] Miguel Santos: Yup. This is where the error messaging needs to carry a “retry-after” or similar signal. Today it doesn’t consistently. We have an internal change in flight to set 429 for policy denies with Retry-After, and reserve 503 for “system can’t serve” cases.

[07:16] Sara Kim: That would help. Our client will honor Retry-After.

[07:19] Logan Wright: Also, we can add a header with a reason code like “burst_pool_saturated” versus “tenant_tps_cap” versus “cooldown_active.” But we’re being careful not to leak anything sensitive.

[07:32] Anita Rao: Please, yes. Even just those three would be great.

[07:36] Miguel Santos: Okay. That’s consistent with what we heard from the other pilot as well.

[07:41] David Chen: And the 503s — should we treat them as retryable? Because we do, but then we got into the retry storm.

[07:49] Peter Holtz: Generally 503 is retryable but you need jitter and a cap. And you need to avoid synchronized retries across your workers. If you can respect Retry-After on 429, that should cut down the storm. For 503, we’re trying to make them rarer and only for real “no route” cases.

[08:08] Miguel Santos: Let’s anchor on one concrete scenario. Yesterday at 8:12 PT, your spike hits. Baseline is full. Burst attempts start. If pool is okay and you’re within caps, you get admitted. If you exceed TPS cap, you get 429 with Retry-After. If the pool saturation gate trips, you also get denied — that one might be 503 today, but we’d like to make it 429 with a different reason code, because it’s basically “temporarily unavailable.”

[08:35] David Chen: From our perspective, 429 is easier, because we treat it as backpressure.

[08:39] Sara Kim: Yeah.

[08:40] Miguel Santos: Great. That’s our direction.

[08:43] Anita Rao: One more thing: can we differentiate baseline throttling vs burst throttling? Like, if baseline is full, we want to know that too.

[08:52] Logan Wright: Internally we can. Externally, we can probably add a response header like “x-redwood-capacity-tier: baseline|burst” for successes. For failures, we can add “x-redwood-deny-scope: baseline|burst.” But we need to confirm naming.

[09:09] Miguel Santos: We’ll take that as a follow-up. For now, let’s focus on deny reason and retry signals.

[09:16] Sara Kim: Ok.

[09:18] Miguel Santos: On the reject rates: do you have a target? Like what’s acceptable during spike?

[09:24] Sara Kim: Honestly, for the pilot, we can tolerate some. But for GA, we’d want it to be like less than 1% for the “contracted” burst amount. If we go above that, we’d rather just buy more baseline.

[09:38] David Chen: Or at least we’d want to know it’s because we exceeded the contracted limit, not because other tenants ate the pool.

[09:46] Miguel Santos: Totally fair. The product goal is: if you’re within the contracted envelope and within guardrails, you should be admitted unless the pool itself is in protection mode. If the pool is in protection mode, we want it to be clearly communicated and relatively rare.

[10:06] Peter Holtz: And that’s where pool sizing comes in. If we see consistent saturation in us-east, we either add capacity to the pool or adjust the eligibility or caps.

[10:17] Sara Kim: Are we allowed to request a dedicated burst pool just for us?

[10:22] Miguel Santos: Not in v1, no. It’s controlled shared. Later we might do customer-managed or fully isolated burst pools, but that’s not in the initial scope.

[10:33] Sara Kim: Okay.

[10:34] Miguel Santos: Let’s talk about your current caps. I don’t want to read them out loud if this is recorded, but roughly: you have a concurrency cap that’s like 2x baseline, and a TPS cap that was set based on your last month p95. Does that sound right?

[10:49] Sara Kim: Yeah, and I think the TPS cap might be low for that spike. Because the spike isn’t “p95,” it’s basically p100 once a day.

[10:58] Anita Rao: And our prompts are longer in the morning because they include overnight context.

[11:05] Logan Wright: That matters. TPS is a function of tokens, not requests. So if your average tokens per request goes up, you hit TPS cap sooner.

[11:14] David Chen: That explains why it was fine last week but not this week — we shipped a feature with longer contexts.

[11:20] Sara Kim: Yeah, we did. That’s probably it.

[11:23] Miguel Santos: Great catch. So two things: (1) we can revisit the TPS cap for the pilot, and (2) we should add better visibility so you can correlate average tokens/request with burst denials.

[11:37] Logan Wright: We have that internally — like tokens per second, tokens per request distribution. We’re careful with cardinality but tenant-level aggregates are fine.

[11:46] Sara Kim: If you can add a simple panel, that’d be great.

[11:49] Miguel Santos: We’ll work on it. For this week, quick mitigation: can you smooth the spike? Like stagger the background jobs by even 2 minutes?

[11:59] Sara Kim: We can try. We can add some jitter to the job scheduler.

[12:03] David Chen: And we can lower the client timeout maybe. Right now it’s like 60 seconds, which is too long when you’re in cooldown.

[12:10] Peter Holtz: Yeah. If you’re denied, you should fail fast and retry later, not hold connections open.

[12:18] Miguel Santos: Let’s pivot to the error messaging you saw. Do you remember the literal text?

[12:23] David Chen: It was something like “Service unavailable.” Not helpful. And one said “upstream connect error” — which sounds like envoy.

[12:32] Peter Holtz: Ah, yeah. That’s likely an internal proxy error message leaking through when routing can’t find an admitted backend. We already have a fix in review to map those to a stable Redwood error response.

[12:45] Miguel Santos: The goal is: you should get a consistent JSON error body with fields like “code,” “message,” and optionally “retry_after_ms.” Plus headers with a reason code. No random envoy text.

[12:59] Sara Kim: That would be much better. Our support team sees those and assumes outage.

[13:04] Miguel Santos: Exactly.

[13:06] Anita Rao: Also can you include in the error whether the request was attempted on baseline and then burst? Like “baseline saturated, burst denied.” That would be… super helpful.

[13:16] Peter Holtz: We can. But we need to be careful that we’re not exposing internal topology. But “baseline saturated” is probably okay because it’s your own dedicated pool.

[13:26] Miguel Santos: I think we can safely include “baseline_at_capacity: true/false” and “burst_attempted: true/false.” Logan, does that cause any logging or metric issues?

[13:35] Logan Wright: No, that’s fine. The bigger risk is making the payload too stable too early. But for pilot, we can add it behind a flag.

[13:44] David Chen: Even if it’s a header, that’s fine.

[13:47] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[13:48] Miguel Santos: On retry guidance: what are you doing today? You mentioned 250ms backoff.

[13:54] David Chen: Yeah. For 429 we do exponential backoff starting at 250ms, max like 3 seconds, up to 5 retries. For 503 we do immediate retry twice, then exponential.

[14:06] Sara Kim: Which, in hindsight, is bad.

[14:08] David Chen: Yeah.

[14:10] Peter Holtz: I’d suggest: treat burst denies like backpressure. Respect Retry-After. If no Retry-After, use a floor like 2 seconds with jitter. And cap retries so you don’t exceed your own concurrency.

[14:24] Miguel Santos: We’ll send a recommended policy in writing. The docs PR is in progress but we can share a draft snippet.

[14:32] Sara Kim: Great.

[14:33] Miguel Santos: Switching gears: did you notice any impact on your neighbor workloads? Like other tenants you manage, or your own other routes?

[14:41] Sara Kim: We only have the one dedicated tenant. But we did see some p99 drift on our chat route when the summarization jobs kick in.

[14:50] Anita Rao: That’s probably just our own contention though.

[14:53] Peter Holtz: Could be. The whole point of the burst design is to protect neighbors, but within your tenant you still share baseline resources across routes unless you separate them.

[15:03] Sara Kim: Right.

[15:04] Miguel Santos: For the pilot we’re not doing per-route burst allocation, but it’s something we’ve talked about for later.

[15:12] David Chen: Another question: if burst pool saturates, does it affect baseline latency? Like do we get slower even on baseline?

[15:20] Peter Holtz: Not directly. The pools are isolated. But at the client level, if you’re retrying a lot, you can increase your own load and that can make baseline look worse. So yes indirectly.

[15:32] David Chen: Makes sense.

[15:34] Miguel Santos: Logan, can you talk about what we can share with them from a metrics standpoint? Like, what panels do we have now and what’s coming.

[15:42] Logan Wright: Yeah. Today, internally, we track: burst_admit_total, burst_deny_total, deny_reason, pool_saturation, tenant_tps, tenant_concurrency, and then latency histograms split by baseline vs burst. In the customer console, we currently only show overall request rate and latency. We’re adding a burst section, but we’re trying to keep dimensions low-cardinality. So likely: tenant+region, maybe model family but not model ID.

[16:09] Sara Kim: We don’t need model ID.

[16:11] Logan Wright: Great. Then we can expose: admit rate, deny rate, and top deny reason codes aggregated. And maybe a simple “burst usage” token counter, but note it’s shadow metered right now.

[16:26] Miguel Santos: Right, shadow metering means we’re attributing usage but not billing you yet.

[16:31] Sara Kim: Yeah, we understand.

[16:33] Anita Rao: But we do want to see it, because we’re doing unit economics work.

[16:37] Miguel Santos: Totally.

[16:39] David Chen: And also, could you give us an alert? Like if deny rate > X% during a window.

[16:45] Peter Holtz: We can set something up on our side and notify you. For customer-facing alerting, it’s not built yet, but we can do an email or Slack webhook in the pilot.

[16:55] Sara Kim: Slack would be great.

[16:57] Miguel Santos: We can do that. Let me check with the team on how we want to operationalize it. We don’t want to spam you.

[17:05] David Chen: Even a daily digest is fine.

[17:08] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[17:10] Miguel Santos: Quick check: any security/compliance concerns come up with burst so far? I know your security team asked earlier about audit logs.

[17:18] Sara Kim: Not new concerns. The main thing is still “does traffic leave the region” and the answer is no.

[17:24] Miguel Santos: Correct. And config changes are audit logged. If we add new headers, we’ll confirm they don’t include anything sensitive.

[17:33] David Chen: Cool.

[17:35] Miguel Santos: Let’s come back to the core issue: the 12% error window. There are a few hypotheses: (1) you hit tenant TPS cap because of longer prompts, (2) pool saturation because other burst tenants spiked, (3) cooldown due to spiky traffic causing repeated denies.

[17:55] Peter Holtz: Once we have the request IDs and I correlate with our reason codes, we’ll know which it is.

[18:02] Sara Kim: If it’s TPS cap, can we raise it?

[18:05] Miguel Santos: For pilot, yes, within reason. We want to preserve neighbor protection, but we can adjust your limits and see if pool stays healthy.

[18:13] Logan Wright: And we can also add a “soft warning” threshold so you see you’re approaching cap before it hard denies. That’s more of a product thing though.

[18:22] Anita Rao: That would be nice. Like a metric that says “cap utilization.”

[18:26] Logan Wright: Exactly. We have it internally, we can expose it.

[18:31] David Chen: If it’s pool saturation, what happens? Do you resize the pool?

[18:36] Miguel Santos: Either resize or adjust eligibility. For example, we may limit burst availability to fewer tenants during a constrained period. But we’d prefer to size to demand if we can.

[18:48] David Chen: Ok.

[18:49] Miguel Santos: Quick question: are you also evaluating other providers for burst-like behavior? Just so we understand expectations.

[18:56] Sara Kim: We looked at Bedrock briefly. But the reason we’re here is dedicated + performance consistency. We don’t want to move.

[19:04] Miguel Santos: Great, thanks.

[19:06] Anita Rao: On error messaging: can we have the error body be stable? Like, we parse it.

[19:12] Miguel Santos: Yes. We’re standardizing. We’ll version it if we need to. We can commit to stable fields for GA.

[19:21] Peter Holtz: Today, I’d avoid parsing free-form message strings. Use code + status + retry-after.

[19:28] David Chen: Sure.

[19:30] Miguel Santos: We’re at the half way point. Anything else you want to cover?

[19:35] Sara Kim: Two things. First, we want to know if the “deny” is happening before we spend tokens. Like, are we being charged? I know it’s shadow metering, but I want to make sure the logic is “admission before compute.”

[19:48] Logan Wright: Yes, admission happens before it enters the generation stage. So denies should not incur token usage. We still count the request, but it’s not token-billed. In shadow metering we’d record zero tokens for those.

[20:02] Sara Kim: Great.

[20:03] Sara Kim: Second, can we get a clearer doc on what “cooldown” values are? Like is it 30 seconds, 60 seconds? Because that impacts our retry policy.

[20:12] Miguel Santos: We can share the current numbers for your tenant. They’re configurable. We might tweak defaults, but we’ll notify you.

[20:20] Peter Holtz: It’s on the order of tens of seconds, not minutes, but yes it’s significant.

[20:26] David Chen: Yesterday it felt like a minute.

[20:29] Peter Holtz: Could be compounded if you keep retrying and keep tripping it.

[20:34] David Chen: Right.

[20:36] Miguel Santos: Okay. We’ll follow up with the actual values.

[20:40] Anita Rao: Another small thing — when it denies, can you also include whether it was concurrency cap vs TPS cap? Because we can fix those differently.

[20:49] Miguel Santos: Yes, that’s basically the deny reason code. We’ll do that.

[20:54] Logan Wright: We’ll aim for a short enum list. Something like: TENANT_CONCURRENCY_LIMIT, TENANT_TPS_LIMIT, POOL_SATURATION_GATE, COOLDOWN_ACTIVE, and maybe CONFIG_DISABLED.

[21:09] Sara Kim: Perfect.

[21:11] Miguel Santos: Peter, do you want to ask anything from SRE perspective?

[21:15] Peter Holtz: Yeah. David, when you saw the spike, did you page internally? Like did it trigger your incident process.

[21:22] David Chen: It did a page because error rate crossed threshold. It was a low-sev, but still a page.

[21:29] Peter Holtz: Would it help if we provided an “expected burst deny” signal, so you can set different thresholds during the window?

[21:37] David Chen: Yes. Even if it’s just a label we can filter on.

[21:41] Logan Wright: That would likely be a metric split. Or you can use the response header to log and create a separate error budget.

[21:49] David Chen: Yeah, we can do that.

[21:51] Miguel Santos: Great.

[21:53] Miguel Santos: Okay, let’s do a quick recap of decisions and next steps before we run out.

[21:58] Miguel Santos: 1) You’ll send 2 request IDs from yesterday’s 8:10-8:25 window.

[22:03] Sara Kim: Yep.

[22:04] Miguel Santos: 2) Peter will pull traces and determine root cause for denials (TPS cap vs pool saturation vs cooldown).

[22:11] Peter Holtz: Yup.

[22:12] Miguel Santos: 3) We’ll share updated retry/backoff guidance, specifically around treating denies as backpressure, honoring Retry-After, and using jitter.

[22:22] David Chen: Great.

[22:23] Miguel Santos: 4) We’ll work on improving error semantics: consistent 429 vs 503, stable JSON body, and add deny reason code headers.

[22:33] Sara Kim: That’s the big one.

[22:35] Miguel Santos: 5) Telemetry: we’ll look at exposing a small set of customer-visible panels: admit/deny, cap utilization, and maybe tokens/request correlation.

[22:47] Logan Wright: Yup.

[22:49] Miguel Santos: Cool.

[22:51] Sara Kim: On the TPS cap, can we preemptively raise it? Or do you want to wait until after trace.

[22:57] Peter Holtz: I’d prefer to confirm first, because if the pool was already at 0.85 saturation, raising your cap might make it worse for everyone. But if it’s purely your cap, we can raise and keep pool safe.

[23:10] Miguel Santos: Let’s wait 24 hours. We’ll have the answer tomorrow.

[23:14] Sara Kim: Okay.

[23:16] David Chen: One more question: if we exceed our contract burst cap, do we get denied, or do we get admitted and then overage billed?

[23:24] Miguel Santos: In v1, it’s strict admission control, so you get denied beyond cap. The reason is to protect neighbors and keep behavior predictable. Longer-term we may support overage with explicit opt-in, but not in this beta.

[23:39] David Chen: Got it.

[23:41] Anita Rao: That’s fine.

[23:43] Miguel Santos: Also, we’re still in shadow billing, so you’ll see usage attribution but no invoice line items yet.

[23:50] Sara Kim: Okay.

[23:52] Miguel Santos: Alright. We’ve got about 15 minutes left. Do you want to walk through the exact client behavior? Sometimes the retry layer is the biggest lever.

[24:01] David Chen: Sure. We use an internal gateway. It pools connections. When it sees 503, it retries immediately on the same upstream, which is not ideal. For 429, it does exponential backoff but doesn’t honor Retry-After because you’re not sending it.

[24:17] Peter Holtz: Yep. That maps.

[24:19] David Chen: If you add Retry-After, we can change it to honor it. And also if you standardize on 429, we can avoid the immediate retry path.

[24:31] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[24:33] Sara Kim: Also, minor thing: we saw “burst denied” sometimes but it wasn’t consistent. Like, I think one response had a header already, but not always.

[24:42] Peter Holtz: That could be because some responses were coming from different layers (proxy vs router). We’ll standardize.

[24:50] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[24:52] Anita Rao: Any ETA on when the error improvements land?

[24:57] Miguel Santos: I don’t want to overpromise, but we’re aiming this week for the stable status code mapping and the headers behind a feature flag. Next week for the customer console panels.

[25:09] Sara Kim: Great.

[25:11] Logan Wright: For console, we might first send you a Grafana snapshot link. The actual console integration takes longer.

[25:19] Sara Kim: That’s fine.

[25:21] Miguel Santos: Okay.

[25:22] David Chen: Can we talk about region? We’re in us-east. If us-east burst pool is saturated, can we optionally fail over to us-west burst? Like as an emergency.

[25:33] Miguel Santos: That’s a bigger discussion. It touches data residency and latency. We can support cross-region fallback only if you explicitly enable it and accept higher latency. It’s not in your current pilot.

[25:47] Sara Kim: For us, not worth it. We’d rather just get denied than violate residency.

[25:52] Miguel Santos: Understood.

[25:54] Peter Holtz: Also cross-region would complicate the “noisy neighbor” protections, because now two pools are involved.

[26:01] David Chen: Makes sense.

[26:03] Miguel Santos: Alright.

[26:04] Miguel Santos: Anything else on your side, before we close?

[26:08] Sara Kim: Not really. The main thing is clarity. If we can tell oncall “this is burst backpressure” we can reduce noise.
